title: Cryptanalysis techniques — Isogeny Labs
description: A working reference on how cryptographic hardness assumptions are actually attacked: generic discrete-log algorithms, index calculus and descent, lattice attacks, and isogeny attacks — with concrete costs and stated limits.
heading:
How these problems
are actually attacked.
standfirst: A security level is a claim about work. This library collects the attacks that claim is measured against — what each one needs, what it costs, and precisely where it stops being relevant. Every page states its assumptions and points at the primary sources rather than restating folklore.
scope: Public-key hardness assumptions, with an ECC and isogeny bias
guide_heading:
Read an attack the way
a parameter-setter does.

guide_blocks.p: Most published attacks do not break anything. They move an exponent, or they require a structural coincidence that real parameters avoid, or they assume an oracle nobody can build. The useful question is never "is this broken?" but "what does this attack cost against my parameters, and what would have to change for it to matter?"
So each page here is organised around four things, in this order:

ul: The problem instance. Exactly what the attacker is given, and what counts as success.
The mechanism. The one idea that makes the attack cheaper than brute force — usually a collision, a relation, or a structure-preserving map to an easier object.
The cost. An asymptotic bound, plus whatever the largest honest computation on record actually consumed.
The boundary. The hypothesis that makes the attack work, and therefore the parameter choice that makes it irrelevant.

guide_blocks.note: An asymptotic complexity is not a security level. A bound of O(√n) group operations says nothing about memory, communication, or the constant in front — and it is those, not the exponent, that decide whether a computation is affordable. Where a record computation exists, its measured resource use is worth more than the bound.

families.label: Generic group algorithms
families.heading: Attacks that use nothing about the group.
families.intro: These work against any cyclic group in which you can multiply and test equality. They set the ceiling every concrete discrete-log parameter is measured against, and Shoup's lower bound says no generic algorithm can do better than √p.

planned.title: Baby-step giant-step and kangaroos
planned.one_liner: Deterministic √n time-memory tradeoffs, and Pollard's lambda method for logarithms known to lie in a short interval.

families.label: Index calculus and descent
families.heading: Attacks that exploit the arithmetic underneath.
families.intro: Index calculus collects multiplicative relations over a factor base and solves a linear system. It is why finite-field discrete logs are subexponential and RSA moduli must be large — and why the question of whether it reaches elliptic curves has occupied two decades of research.

planned.title: The number field sieve
planned.one_liner: The subexponential L(1/3) algorithm behind factoring and prime-field discrete-log records, and what its precomputation phase means for reused parameters.

planned.title: Gröbner-basis solving and first fall degree
planned.one_liner: How F4/F5 behaves on the polynomial systems that index calculus generates, and why the measured degree of regularity decides feasibility.

families.label: Lattice attacks
families.heading: Attacks that turn partial information into a short vector.
families.intro: When a secret is almost known — a few leaked bits, a slightly biased nonce, a small root of a modular equation — lattice reduction usually finishes the job. These are the attacks that break deployed systems whose underlying mathematics was never in question.

planned.title: Coppersmith's method
planned.one_liner: Finding small roots of modular polynomials, and the partial-key-exposure and small-exponent attacks on RSA that follow from it.

families.label: Isogeny attacks
families.heading: Attacks on the newest assumptions.
families.intro: Isogeny problems are the youngest hardness assumptions in deployment-adjacent cryptography, and the only ones to have had a headline scheme broken outright after standardisation review had begun. That history is the argument for reading them carefully rather than the argument for avoiding them.

planned.title: Kuperberg's algorithm and CSIDH
planned.one_liner: Subexponential quantum attacks on the class-group action, and the parameter dispute they caused.

planned.title: Meet-in-the-middle and the supersingular path problem
planned.one_liner: Delfs–Galbraith, claw finding, and what the √p barrier means for SQIsign parameters.
